stories.topic: A thank-you note, two decades late
stories.summary: Amit plays a video message from one of his writing students, Uja Sharma. Around 2000–2001, as a final-year student at the College of Business Studies in Delhi University, she was doing a project on futures and options and found that 90% of her research material carried Ajay's name. She emailed him without expecting a reply. He answered promptly and spent more than an hour on a video call explaining how derivatives worked, how the policy was coming together and what NSE was doing. She aced the subject. The memory had faded on Ajay's side, but Amit says it 'clearly happened' and is exactly the kind of thing Ajay does.
stories.insight: Small acts of intellectual generosity can shape someone for decades without the giver ever knowing. The person who was helped remembers, and passes it on.
stories.quote: I think that experience taught me that it's very important to make time for young people and it stayed with me because every time a young person reaches out to me, I make time for them now.

stories.topic: Ajay discovers his dharma as a help desk
stories.summary: In the late 1990s, derivatives trading was taking off in India. Ajay did seminars across the country and a series of tutorial-style TV conversations that were replayed twice a day, so people came to see him as the teacher of derivatives. Then strangers began emailing him their plans and their problems and asking him to fix them. At first he was taken aback, since he was not going to debug other people's work. By the fifth email he decided this was his calling. He has replied carefully to such emails ever since, and makes time for PhD students and early-career academics too.
stories.insight: When the same kind of request keeps arriving at your door, it may be telling you where you are most useful. Accepting that role can quietly do a lot of public good.
stories.quote: But by the fifth email, I got the message that the good Lord had intended for me to be a help desk. So I decided to discharge my dharma and I faithfully replied to all these emails.

stories.topic: Amit Varma as a Design One firm
stories.summary: Hearing Ajay describe the firm where one person owns 100% and is also the CEO, Amit recognises his own life. He thinks of every creator as an entrepreneur running their own brand, both shareholder and CEO, and compares himself to Travis Bickle talking to the mirror in Taxi Driver. The upside is total alignment: he follows his own vision and has passed up big opportunities to do what he loves. The downsides are that he cannot scale and is limited by his own imagination and knowledge, with no advisors to see further ahead.
stories.insight: The episode's ideas about firm design apply to individual careers too. A solo creator gets perfect alignment but pays for it in scale and blind spots. Ajay adds that employees wouldn't fix this, because people rarely challenge a 100% owner.
stories.quote: I think of every creator as being an entrepreneur of his own brand. So in everything I do, I am basically the person.

stories.topic: Tom Watson Jr's giant gamble at IBM
stories.summary: Tom Watson Jr inherited IBM from his father, its founder. At the time IBM was a feudal sort of company where employees sang the company anthem every morning. The son bet on the world's most expensive operating system project, OS/360, which in inflation-adjusted dollars cost more than the Manhattan Project. He led IBM through it.
stories.insight: Family heirs are not always timid caretakers. A successor with hunger and skin in the game can take bet-the-company risks, which is exactly what Ajay says owner-run firms usually fail to do.
stories.quote: And Tom Watson Jr, the son, rolled the dice on the world's most expensive operating system project.

stories.topic: Shamin Desai's film class at Channel V
stories.summary: Amit worked at Channel V from 1995 to 1997, his second job. There a filmmaker named Shamin Desai, who sadly died a few years ago, gathered five or six people from the promos department for an informal film-appreciation session. He explained that Coppola made Rumblefish at the same time as The Outsiders, with almost the same cast. He argued that Rumblefish was a masterpiece, then played it for them. Amit remembers it as a masterclass in film appreciation.
stories.insight: Amit links the memory back to the episode's theme: a senior person taking time to teach juniors is what good corporate culture looks like. It echoes Ajay's help-desk story.
stories.quote: And he said Rumblefish is a masterpiece, spoke all about it, and played it. And there were just like five or six of us.

recommendations.item: Father, Son & Co: My Life at IBM and Beyond
recommendations.creator: Thomas J Watson Jr
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode. It is the memoir of the son who inherited IBM from its founder.
recommendations.reason: A purely family-business book, about Designs One and Two rather than the modern firm, and beautifully written. It covers how Watson Jr took over a feudal company and bet it on OS/360. Ajay read it when he was young and says it gave him great insight into the challenges of running a family business.

recommendations.creator: Mario Puzo
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, chosen to fit the episode's family theme. Ajay promptly produced a copy from his shelf.
recommendations.reason: It is a story about a family enterprise. Amit calls the book 'bloody good' and counts it, along with the films, among the masterpieces.

recommendations.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
recommendations.context: Part of Amit's recommendation: a legendary 1970s film that won many Oscars.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece about a family enterprise, and Coppola at his absolute peak.

recommendations.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
recommendations.context: Recommended with the first film. Amit notes it also won Oscars.
recommendations.reason: Amit says both films are masterpieces and that together they are Coppola at his peak.

recommendations.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
recommendations.context: Came up while Amit was praising Coppola. It triggered his memory of Shamin Desai's film-appreciation session at Channel V.
recommendations.reason: Amit loved it, and Desai convinced that small room it was a masterpiece. It is also tied to a memory Amit treasures about mentorship and good culture.

recommendations.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. In the anecdote, it is the film Coppola made alongside Rumblefish with pretty much the same cast.
recommendations.reason: Worth knowing as the companion piece to Rumblefish. Amit does not praise it separately.

recommendations.item: What You Can Learn from Family Business
recommendations.creator: Nicolas Kachaner, George Stalk Jr, and Alain Bloch
recommendations.context: A Harvard Business Review piece Amit cites. He notes that Indians look down on family firms but look up to Western media that give gyan.
recommendations.reason: It counters the stereotype with evidence from family firms worldwide. Professionally run firms do better in good times, but family firms do less badly in bad times. Family firms are frugal, keep a high bar for capital expenditure and carry little debt. They make fewer and smaller acquisitions, are surprisingly diversified and international, and retain talent better. Ajay says he agrees with all of it.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended when Ajay explained that firms with dispersed shareholding and no promoter have only begun appearing in India in the last 10–15 years.
recommendations.reason: The earlier episode on the history and evolution of finance covers this shift in great detail.

core_ideas.concept: Think in incentives, not class stereotypes
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that India has a kind of caste system in business. People look down on traditional business families and revere the IIT-certified professional. They assume family managers are second-rate and that hiring a professional will solve everything. His thesis is that this is the wrong lens. The right one looks at the forces that produce good and bad decisions inside a firm: alignment, skin in the game, time horizons, risk appetite and how power is spread. On those terms a family CEO can beat a professional CEO, or lose to one.
core_ideas.quote: And my core thesis for today is that this is the wrong way to think about the world, and we should think about incentives, we should think about the forces that create good and bad decisions inside firms.

core_ideas.concept: Design One: the founder as 'little deity'
core_ideas.explanation: The founder owns 100% and is also the CEO. Incentives are perfectly aligned, and the owner will work flat out. The cost is that nobody can check the founder. No one disagrees or forces a debate, so bad projects get picked and money gets wasted. Having employees doesn't fix this, because people rarely challenge someone who owns 100% of the firm.
core_ideas.quote: In this firm, you are the little deity, you are the God, you do all the thinking, you make all the decisions, there is no check and balance, there is nobody to restrain you, there is nobody to disagree with you,

core_ideas.explanation: When most of an owner's wealth, ego and social standing is tied up in one firm, they become risk-averse. They make only small, incremental changes and avoid the big bets that transform a business. Capitalism needs those gambles: some firms succeed wildly and many die, and that creative destruction is healthy. Owner-run firms that won't take such bets fall behind as markets and technology change. The flaw is the structure, not the person.
core_ideas.quote: The only way to build a great business is to roll the dice and to take risks, to take important risks, to take earth shaking gambles on the way of firm works.

core_ideas.concept: Design Two: minority shareholders and the narrow Indian debate
core_ideas.explanation: The founder keeps 60% and stays CEO, while outside investors hold 40%, possibly through an IPO. This is common among listed Indian family firms. Alignment stays high and the founder is slightly more diversified, but power is just as concentrated and the founder remains risk-averse. A new problem appears: a 60% owner can take more than 60% of the cash, so minority investors pay less for the shares. Ajay says most Indian company law and SEBI rules for listed firms target this one issue, and miss the bigger flaws of under-diversification and excessive power.
core_ideas.quote: So there is an attempt by the Indian state at fighting this narrow battle that how do we make sure that the 40% minority shareholders get forty percent of the cash? That's all.

core_ideas.explanation: The family keeps 60% and hires a salaried 'professional' CEO with no equity, a move the Indian elite tends to applaud. But that CEO has no skin in the game, and their career incentives push toward caution. In a typical five-year term, the first three years go into avoiding the sack through cost control and small improvements. They then squeak through to a second term and coast to year ten without rocking the boat. The 60% chairman, who hires them and can fire them, also nudges them away from risk and is unlikely to be stopped from taking extra cash. Meanwhile the CEO consolidates power inside the firm with no one to question them.
core_ideas.quote: So having an IIT degree doesn't change things. It's an incentives question. So design three actually achieves very little.

core_ideas.concept: Design Four: dispersed shareholding plus a strong board
core_ideas.explanation: This is how mature firms around the world work. There is no promoter. Shares are spread across institutions and the public, which has only started happening in India in the last 10–15 years. Shareholders pick a board of about seven people: the CEO, roughly three shareholder directors whose 5–15% stakes matter to them, and roughly three independent directors. The board sets strategy and organisation design, hires the CEO, decides their pay and holds them accountable. Sometimes the board makes things so hot that the CEO leaves, and Ajay calls that healthy. Stock options give the CEO a reason to chase upside, and diversified shareholders can accept that some firms fail. Ajay stresses that this is culture, not law, and takes decades to build.
core_ideas.quote: But the strategy of the firm is controlled by the board, where the CEO is a member. That CEO is one out of the seven. But the CEO doesn't control the strategy of the firm.

core_ideas.concept: Concentrated power and the great-man myth
core_ideas.explanation: The business world credits success to a visionary CEO and blames failure on a bad one. Ajay says much of the outcome is luck and forces outside the firm, such as being in the right industry at the right time, or the world suddenly changing. The world is too complicated for any single mind. Better decisions, and the ability to admit and fix mistakes, come only from many minds debating. People also tend to behave worse when they hold concentrated power. Indian business, he says, is still stuck in a 'primitive great man theory'.
core_ideas.quote: It is only by harnessing many, many minds that we have a hope of understanding the world better and making better decisions, making fewer mistakes, being able to self-correct,

core_ideas.concept: Build the board before you hire the outsider
core_ideas.explanation: For a family firm moving toward Design Four, Ajay suggests an order. First spread out the shareholding and build the board as a real institution, with about three shareholder directors and three independents. Only after that bring in a professional CEO. Power in the hands of an aligned family member is relatively safe. Power in the hands of an unchecked hired manager is the real worry. Outside strategy advisors help by challenging the existing management. All this requires the current CEO to give up power, which is rare: Ajay has sat on more than 20 boards and seen 'disgusting levels of arrogance' in CEOs.
core_ideas.quote: It may make sense to first build a board as an institution.

core_ideas.concept: Execution is management's comfort zone; strategy is the hard part
core_ideas.explanation: Indian managements retreat into execution because strategy means facing an unpredictable world and making difficult calls. A board and strategy advisors exist to pull management out of that comfort zone. They push for transformation, such as demanding growth of five times, rather than small step-by-step improvements.
core_ideas.quote: The curse of India is managements want to do execution, it's their comfort zone. You go home and watch TV, you don't have to think too much.

core_ideas.concept: Family wealth fades across generations, so plan the path to Design Four
core_ideas.explanation: Amit cites a worldwide pattern: when a family becomes wealthy, about 70% of that wealth is lost by the next generation and about 90% by the one after. Ajay's answer is that if a family member has the hunger and ability, a family-led path toward Design Four beats handing the firm to a professional. Many families lack such a successor, though. Others are pushed into dispersed shareholding by their history, for example when venture capital and private equity investors exit after an IPO. Then making Design Four work is the only option.
core_ideas.quote: When a family becomes wealthy, 70% of that wealth is lost by the next generation, 90% is lost by the generation after that.

core_ideas.concept: Rich countries are built of sophisticated firms
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says India's path from poor to rich runs through its firms. Public policy can only create the right conditions and nudge a little. The real change is cultural: norms, how power works in the boardroom, and how the seven people in that room behave. That journey has to be made by the Indian elite.
core_ideas.quote: A rich country is made of sophisticated firms. A poor country is made of bad firms.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on becoming the nation's derivatives help desk: 'by the fifth email, I got the message that the good Lord had intended for me to be a help desk. So I decided to discharge my dharma.'

Ajay's running example is the fictional 'Amitbhai Media Limited'. After Designs Two and Three each make things worse, Amit pleads: 'And now we need to get to design four, please save Amitbhai Media Limited.'
Ajay mocking Indian reverence for entrance exams: there is 'the instinctive respect that somebody who could solve maths problems in 12th standard is a cool guy.'

Amit, as Ajay takes apart the professional CEO: 'At this point, I must point out to gentle readers that our good friend Ajay Bhai Shah is from IIT, right? So he is a professional, and he's coming to my family firm... This is most insidious, but continue.'
After a cat-like scream is heard in the background, Amit tells listeners it wasn't a cat: 'It was a wailing of a CEO who had been ejected by the animal behavior of an unruly board.'

When Ajay instantly produces a copy of The Godfather, Amit is stunned: 'Oh you have it. What the fuck? You have everything here.' He wonders whether Ajay owns something that looks like a book but has a screen, so any book Amit names just appears on it.
Taxi Driver: Amit compares himself, as both shareholder and CEO of his own one-person firm, to Travis Bickle in front of the mirror ('You're talking to me?'), adding 'I can't act, of course.'
Steve Jobs as the poster child of the visionary-CEO myth. Ajay's rebuttal: 'Steve Jobs made many, many wrong decisions. He almost took Apple into bankruptcy.'
IBM's OS/360 under Tom Watson Jr cost more in inflation-adjusted dollars than the Manhattan Project. Also the old IBM, where people sang the company anthem every morning.
The Nehrus as an example of decline across generations: 'Motilal Nehru downwards, they just kind of got lesser and lesser as people.'
Dhirubhai and Mukesh Ambani: 'every Dhirubhai is not going to have a Mukesh. You know, that was just getting extraordinarily lucky.'
